items.detail: September opened with a much heavier version of Monday's selloff — the **S&P 500 fell 0.71% to 7,631.47**, the **Nasdaq dropped 271 points (1.03%) to 26,099.77** and the **Dow lost 419 points (0.79%) to 52,766.88**, roughly doubling the previous session's decline.
items.why: Two supertankers were struck exiting the Strait of Hormuz overnight, which pushed crude and Treasury yields sharply higher together and hardened the view that the Fed will raise rates this month rather than hold.

items.detail: The Hormuz escalation moved from military bases to the tankers themselves — the Saudi-flagged **Sidr** and Liberian-flagged **Senegal Prosperity**, each carrying about **2 million barrels of Saudi crude**, were hit by projectiles minutes apart off Khasab, Oman, sending **Brent up 2% to above $92** and **WTI to roughly $88**.
items.why: Rockets striking loaded VLCCs in the waterway itself converts the war premium from a threat of disruption into evidence of actual disruption, so the market is now pricing physical risk to the roughly one-fifth of global crude that transits Hormuz.

items.detail: The equity selloff was really a bond selloff — the **10-year Treasury yield hit about 4.81%**, its highest since January 2025, and the **30-year climbed to 5.28%**, while **September hike odds jumped to 66.4%** on CME FedWatch from roughly 58% a day earlier.
items.why: An energy supply shock feeds straight into inflation expectations, and with Warsh already signalling that short rates remain the Fed's predominant tool, the curve repriced a September tightening as the base case rather than a coin flip.

items.detail: Tuesday's data did nothing to slow the repricing — **ISM Manufacturing slipped to 54.6** in August from July's near four-year high of 55.6 and below the 55.2 consensus, while **JOLTS openings rose to 7.271 million** from 7.182 million but missed the 7.300 million estimate.
items.why: Both prints were soft enough to signal a cooling economy yet nowhere near weak enough to give the Fed a labour-market excuse to stand pat against an oil-driven inflation impulse, so the hawkish path survived intact.

items.detail: Energy was again the only real place to hide — the sector **rose 1.3%** as one of just four of the eleven S&P groups to finish higher, and the **XLE energy ETF hit a new all-time intraday high** dating back to its 1998 inception, now up roughly **45% year to date** after a **7.02% August**.
items.why: Every dollar of the Hormuz risk premium flows directly into energy earnings estimates, making the sector the mechanical offset to the same shock that is lifting the discount rate on the rest of the index.

items.detail: Gold extended its counter-intuitive war slide for a third session — spot fell **1.60% to $4,374.54**, its **lowest level since August 19**, with **silver down 2.7%** alongside it.
items.why: The tanker strikes raised the odds of a Fed hike rather than a cut, and rising real yields with a firmer dollar outweigh the safe-haven bid for an asset that pays no coupon.

items.detail: Wednesday's open was the capitulation Tuesday avoided — the **Sensex fell 472.96 points (0.61%) to 76,471.32** and the **Nifty dropped 196.60 points to 23,859.20**, breaking decisively below the **23,900** level that had been the line in focus.
items.why: Crude jumped more than $4 a barrel to a five-week high after the Hormuz tanker strikes, and for a net oil importer that lands simultaneously on the import bill, the inflation path and the currency, so the selling was broad rather than sector-specific.

items.detail: Tuesday itself was a near-flat second down day that masked violent stock-level moves — the **Sensex slipped just 12.99 points (0.02%) to 76,944.28** and the **Nifty50 eased 24.60 points (0.10%) to 24,055.80**, with selling in banks, autos and healthcare offset by tech and heavyweights.
items.why: The strong 7.8% GDP print and index-rebalancing flows were still cushioning the benchmark against the oil shock at that point, which is why the damage stayed inside the sector rotation rather than showing up at the index level.

items.detail: The dispersion under the flat tape was extreme — **Maruti Suzuki fell more than 4%** as the worst Nifty performer after August sales showed **exports down over 7% year-on-year**, with Nestle India (-4.01%) and Asian Paints (-3.42%) alongside it, against **ITC +4.23%**, **Adani Ports +3.45%** and **Bharti Airtel +3.10%**.
items.why: Autos carry both the input-cost hit from crude and a softening export channel, while ITC and Bharti are the classic domestic-cashflow defensives investors rotate into when an external shock hits an import-dependent market.

items.detail: The rupee's four-session winning run is ending — it **settled at 94.95 on Tuesday** after touching a **two-month high of 94.80** intraday, but is set to **open lower around 95.02-95.06** on Wednesday.
items.why: The RBI's intervention and index-rejig inflows were enough to push the rupee through 95 while oil was near $90, but a jump to $92 plus a 4.8% US 10-year yield puts both the import bill and the rate differential back against the currency.

items.detail: The damage rotated from metals to rate-sensitives and exporters — **Nifty Realty fell nearly 2%**, **Nifty IT dropped 1.82%** and **Nifty Auto lost 1.78%**, with breadth clearly negative at **2,180 decliners against 1,336 advancers** on the NSE.
items.why: Realty is the most direct casualty of a global yield spike, IT tracks the Nasdaq's 1% fall overnight, and autos are absorbing the crude pass-through, so the three worst sectors map exactly onto the three channels the oil shock travels through.

items.detail: The offshore read stayed weak through the morning — **GIFT Nifty traded at 23,939.5, down 0.47%** from a 24,052 previous close, after an intraday range of 23,907.5 to 24,079.
items.why: Asian risk pricing is tracking the overnight Wall Street decline and the bond selloff rather than any domestic development, leaving India's own growth story sidelined for a second straight session.

items.detail: Monday's short-covering bounce did not hold — **Bitcoin fell 1.6% to $76,988**, back through the range floor, with **Ether down 2.4% to $2,403.43** and **Solana sliding 3.72% to $99.82**, dragging total crypto market cap down **1.4% to $2.7 trillion**.
items.why: The Hormuz tanker strikes pushed the US 10-year yield to about 4.81% and September Fed hike odds to 66.4%, and a rising real-rate path is the single most direct headwind for the highest-beta liquidity assets.

items.detail: Solana broke the psychological line the others held — it is the worst performer of the majors on the day and has now given up **roughly 40% in 2026**, against Ether's 37% decline, even as Bitcoin's year-to-date drawdown remains the shallowest of the group.
items.why: Solana carries the highest beta to liquidity of the three, so a repricing of the Fed path hits it hardest, and its retail-heavy order book offers less institutional bid to absorb the selling than Bitcoin's ETF complex does.

items.detail: The ETF bid returned but was overwhelmed — **spot Bitcoin funds took in $142 million on September 1**, reversing the prior session's $201.9 million outflow, yet BTC still **slipped below $77,500** on the day.
items.why: Regulated inflows of that size are a fraction of the macro repricing driving spot, so a positive flow signal was not enough to offset a bond selloff and a two-thirds probability of a Fed hike.

items.detail: The Bitcoin-Ether divergence has now run long enough to be a trend rather than a blip — **spot Ether ETFs extended their inflow streak to eleven consecutive days**, drawing roughly **$1.6 billion across the run** with no fund reporting an outflow.
items.why: Ether allocators are still building positions on the CFTC digital-commodity classification and staking-yield case, and that structural bid has proved insensitive to the same Fed repricing that broke Bitcoin's nine-day creation streak.

items.detail: Solana's institutional channel stalled abruptly — **spot SOL ETFs took in just $925,000 as September opened**, a collapse from the $33.49 million session that was the largest since mid-December 2025, though cumulative flows stand at **$1.30 billion** through August 28.
items.why: The daily figure is dominated by a small number of allocators, so a single quiet session on a 3.7% down day is enough to take flows to near zero without any change in the longer-term product story.

items.detail: Positioning is unusually clean going into the test — **futures open interest sits near $25.3 billion**, up only 0.6-0.9% in 24 hours, with **average funding at 0.0066% per eight hours**, below the 0.01% baseline, and liquidation clusters concentrated in the **$76,500-$77,000** band that Bitfinex flags at **$77,100**.
items.why: Leverage was flushed out by the $547 million liquidation cascade in late August and has not rebuilt, which means a break of the support band would be driven by spot selling rather than another forced-unwind spiral.

crossCuttingTheme: Rockets hitting two loaded supertankers off Khasab turned the Hormuz war premium from a threat into an event, and the transmission ran entirely through rates rather than growth: Brent above $92 triggered a global bond selloff that took the US 10-year to 4.81% and the 30-year to 5.28%, lifting September Fed hike odds to 66.4% and hitting every long-duration asset at once — the S&P 500 down 0.71% to 7,631.47 with only energy higher, gold down 1.60% to a two-week low instead of rallying on war, Bitcoin back through $77,000 despite $142 million of ETF inflows, and India, the most oil-exposed of the three, gapping below 23,900 with realty, IT and autos each down close to 2%.
